name: Tanning accelerator

lead: Tanning accelerators are lotions (and sometimes pills) marketed to indoor and outdoor tanners to make a tan appear faster or darker. They typically contain the amino acid tyrosine, psoralens or other chemicals, and are meant to be used together with UV exposure.

Marketing holds that tyrosine, a building block of melanin, increases pigment production; encyclopedic sources say no scientific data supports that claim. Psoralens such as 5-methoxypsoralen are photosensitizing compounds used medically in psoriasis and vitiligo, and have also been described as tanning accelerators.

paras: People apply the lotion before sun or sunbed sessions, or take pills in the run-up to tanning. A 2015 survey of 200 indoor tanners found just over half used accelerators and that users tended to tan more often.

In the 2015 survey, acne and rashes were more common among users, and adverse reactions stopped further use about 31 percent of the time. Psoralens are photosensitizers, and a rhesus monkey study found a high share of topically applied 5-methoxypsoralen was absorbed. Accelerators are used with UV exposure, a documented cause of skin cancer.

angle.text: Users apply or take tanning accelerators hoping to darken faster and deeper during UV exposure by boosting melanin production. Wikipedia notes no scientific data supports the melanin claim, and survey users report acne and rashes.

lead: Tanning accelerators, also called tan enhancers or tan extenders, are lotions (and in some cases pills) marketed to people who tan in the sun or in sunbeds. Makers say they help a tan appear sooner or look deeper. They usually contain the amino acid tyrosine, psoralens or other ingredients, and they are meant to be used together with UV exposure, often as the first lotion in an indoor-tanning routine.[1][2][3]

The appeal for appearance is straightforward: a darker, more even tan in fewer sessions. Tyrosine is the raw material from which skin builds melanin, which is the logic behind the marketing, and psoralens such as 5-methoxypsoralen (bergapten) are photosensitising compounds that interact with UV light.[2][3] Some products also add bronzers or warming agents, and patent filings describe compositions that combine an accelerator with a bronzer.[4]

Research on accelerators is limited. The main human study is a 2015 survey of 200 indoor tanners, and the main laboratory work is a study of skin absorption of 5-methoxypsoralen in monkeys; no controlled trial of their tanning effect was found.[1][2]

Sunless tanners (DHA), which need no UV

paras: Tanning accelerators are sold alongside indoor tanning lotions, often applied first in a routine. Some contain bronzers, which colour the skin immediately, and warming or tingle agents; patent filings describe emulsions that combine a tanning accelerator, a bronzer and a warming agent such as an alkyl ether of vanillyl alcohol.[4]

They are distinct from sunless tanning products, which use dihydroxyacetone (DHA) at roughly 3 to 5 percent to react with skin proteins and darken the surface without UV, or oral carotenoid products that tint the skin.[3] Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning places psoralens within the literature on agents that trigger melanogenesis.[3]

Skin tans through melanocytes, which make melanin in two forms, red pheomelanin and dark brown eumelanin; melanin absorbs UV radiation.[5] Wikipedia explains that UVA mainly darkens melanin already present, giving a quick tan that fades, while UVB damages DNA and triggers new melanin production, producing a delayed tan that appears after two or three days and lasts weeks or months.[5] Accelerator marketing targets this process, with products pitched as supplying raw material or sensitising skin so that the same UV exposure gives more colour.[2][3]

sections.h: Ingredients and how they are said to work
paras: Tyrosine, the amino acid that melanocytes convert to melanin, is the best-known accelerator ingredient; marketing says that applying it provides building material for pigment. Wikipedia's sunless tanning article does not describe a documented tanning effect from this approach.[3]

5-Methoxypsoralen (bergapten) is a furanocoumarin first isolated from bergamot essential oil in 1834. It occurs in citrus and carrot-family plants and sensitises skin to UV light.[6] It has been used in psoriasis and vitiligo treatment and has been described as a sun-tanning accelerator.[2][6] The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies it as probably carcinogenic to humans on animal evidence, and contact with plant material containing it followed by UV exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis.[6]

Before the 1920s in the US and Western Europe, tanned skin was associated with outdoor labour, and a tan became fashionable in the 1920s after Coco Chanel's tan and the popularity of Josephine Baker, according to Wikipedia.[5] Jean Patou launched the first sun tan oil, Huile de Chaldee, in 1927, and baby oil was widely used in the 1950s to deepen a tan.[5] Indoor tanning in the late 1970s created a market of bronzers, intensifiers and accelerators sold beside salon beds.[7][5]

Psoralen-based tanning activators also circulated; Wikipedia says health authorities banned psoralen in July 1996 because of photocarcinogenic concerns.[5] Today tanning accelerators are generally tyrosine-based or proprietary blends, and their ingredient lists vary between brands.[1][3]

Wikipedia's sunless tanning article describes several neighbours of the accelerator category. Temporary bronzers are tints that wash off and are used for one-day colour or to complement a DHA tan. DHA self-tanners date to Man-Tan in 1959 and Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960, and automated spray booths broadened the market from the late 1990s.[3] Tanning pills based on beta-carotene or canthaxanthin are not approved by the FDA as tanning agents, and the agency has issued warnings about canthaxanthin, which is linked to orange-brown colouring and retinal deposits.[3]

Melanocortin-based injectables such as melanotan, developed from alpha-MSH analogs at the University of Arizona in the 1980s, are also discussed in tanning communities; Wikipedia reports that health agencies began issuing warnings in 2007 about unlicensed products.[3] These work through a different route from topical accelerators.

Neither bronzer nor sunless tanner is legally defined, and the FDA regulates DHA as a color additive.[3] Accelerators themselves are sold as cosmetics or tanning-salon products and have no dedicated regulation described in the cited sources. Regulation of the exposure they accompany is stronger: the FDA reclassified tanning beds in 2014 and requires a warning against use by under-18s, and France, Brazil and Australia restrict commercial tanning.[7]

Accelerators are marketed mainly in the context of indoor tanning. Friedrich Wolff, often called the father of indoor tanning, developed sunbeds emitting mostly UVA, and the first salon opened in Berlin in 1977, with devices reaching the United States in 1978.[7] Use is most common among white women aged 16 to 25.[7] The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, and meta-analyses have reported higher melanoma risk among ever-users of sunbeds.[7]

The FDA reclassified tanning beds as moderate risk in 2014 and requires a black box warning against use by anyone under 18. Several jurisdictions, including France, Brazil and Australia, have banned or restricted commercial tanning.[7]

No controlled human trial of tanning accelerators was found. The 2015 survey did not test efficacy and did not examine exact ingredients.[1] Wikipedia's sunless tanning article reports no data that tyrosine boosts melanin formation when applied this way.[3]

In the 2015 survey, acne and rashes were more common among accelerator users, and adverse reactions stopped further use 31 percent of the time.[1] Psoralens sensitise skin to UV, and the monkey study's authors described its findings on skin absorption as part of the compound's dermatotoxic profile.[2] UV exposure and sunbeds are established risk factors for melanoma and other skin cancers.[7]

Tanning appears in appearance discussions as a way to look healthier or more defined, and accelerator lotions are part of the product shelf in that conversation. Specific forum threads on accelerators are sparse, so most of what is known about use comes from the 2015 survey of indoor tanners, in which just over half used them, users tanned more often and showed more signs of tanning addiction.[1] Users who prefer a tan without UV turn to bronzers or DHA self-tanners instead.[3]

No studies found testing the effectiveness of tanning accelerators in controlled human trials. Related research includes a cross-sectional survey of 200 indoor tanners, in which 53 percent used accelerators, 97 percent of respondents were female and the median age was 22. Users were more likely to spray tan, tan frequently and report tanning addiction, and acne and rashes were more common among them. The authors noted a limited adult sample and unexamined ingredients.[1]

In animal work, a study in three rhesus monkeys found that after topical application of radiolabelled 5-methoxypsoralen, about 58 percent of the dose was excreted, compared with about 72 percent after injection, indicating high absorption through the skin.[2]

lore.intro: Tanning accelerators are discussed mainly in tanning-salon and sun-care contexts, where users and sellers describe faster or darker tans; published research is limited to a single survey and a monkey absorption study.[1][2]

claims.claim: Tyrosine lotion gives skin more raw material, so you tan faster or darker.
Accelerators let you tan with fewer sessions.
Psoralen-based activators are an effective tanning shortcut.
A bronzer or DHA tanner gives the look without UV.
